title: Students Should Only Use AI for Things They Already Know How to Do Well
author: Daniel Willingham
summary: Cognitive scientist Daniel Willingham lays out a guiding principle for classroom AI policy: students should only use AI for tasks they already know how to perform well. He argues that most district AI guidelines borrow a workplace model, in which AI acts as an associate and the human stays the accountable lead, but that model misapplies to school because the point of a school assignment is never the product itself, it is the mental work the task forces students to do. Using the analogy of calculator use in math class, Willingham contends that AI should replace effort only once mastery has already reduced that effort's learning value, not before. He works through two objections, that AI can scaffold learning for novices, and that even competent students need more practice, and rejects both because novices cannot direct AI usefully and repeated practice is exactly the mental work that produces durable skill. The piece closes by distinguishing life-after-school AI use, where the product matters, from school AI use, where the process is the entire point.
points: Willingham's litmus test reframes the AI debate around learning value rather than honesty or citation: AI is appropriate only for tasks a student could already do unaided, making the standard developmental rather than procedural.

He identifies a category error in most district AI policies: they borrow the 'use AI, but show your work' associate model from the post-graduation workplace, where the product is the goal, and misapply it to school, where the process is the goal.

His rebuttal to the 'AI as scaffold for novices' argument is that novices lack the domain knowledge to prompt AI usefully, so AI tends to hand a novice a polished answer rather than productive struggle.

Writing is his central case study: AI eliminated the one tool teachers had to force students through the cognitive integration, argumentation, and audience-awareness work that a substantial paper requires, and no replacement tool has emerged.
The calculator analogy gives teachers a concrete operational rule: permit the tool once arithmetic (or any component skill) is mastered, withhold it while that skill is still being built.
quotes: Students should only use AI for things that they already know how to do well.
Learning is a product of engaging in mental work, and students may use AI to replace that mental work and hence, not to learn.

No one wants to read the papers they write, and the math problems they solve have no practical value. Teachers have them do these tasks because they provide practice in cognitive abilities that we think matter.
For many educators, writing papers was the only tool we had to ensure that students engage these cognitive processes. AI took that tool from us, and we don't know of a good replacement.
Artificial Intelligence tools should not substitute for tasks wherein students would benefit from doing the mental work themselves.
The novice doesn't know enough to ask good questions. He will give the AI system a vague prompt about the goal of the exercise whereupon AI will sharpen it for the user.

We've all heard "They're going to have to learn to use AI." But I think that slogan applies to how students will use AI at home and in the workforce, where the product is the thing. For students, learning is the thing.
